title: Captain America
subtitle: Marvel's main continuity — the shield, not the man
blurb: 611 issues, from the 1964 revival to the last page Ed Brubaker wrote, one section per run.
notes: 1 is the readable path: the 1964 revival, Steranko, Englehart, Kirby's return, Stern and Byrne, and Brubaker's run from volume five #1 to Winter Soldier #14, where he leaves it. 2 is strongly recommended — DeMatteis, Gruenwald's ten years, Waid, and Captain America and Bucky, the companion book Brubaker co-wrote alongside volume six. 3 is genuinely optional, and most of it is there so the numbering has no holes in it. The minimum viable path is Tier 1 alone.

Captain America #22–24 are chapters of the 2006 crossover and live on the Civil War list here instead, where they sit interleaved with the rest of that event. They are not repeated on this list, which is why this one steps from #21 straight to #25.
Tales of Suspense was a split book.

For #59–99 Captain America has the back half of each issue and Iron Man has the front. Only the back half is on this list, but the issue is one object on a shelf and in Marvel Unlimited, so it is one row.

Sections link the series rather than the issue, because Marvel only exposes the most recent issues of a series to the outside world. The issue numbers are the part you need; the volume changes are the part that catches people out, and the rows name the volume every time it moves.

Issue numbers, cover dates and writer credits machine-read from the Marvel Database (marvel.fandom.com) — the volume page lists say which issues exist and each issue's infobox says who wrote it, and every run boundary below is checked against those credits at build time. Series links resolve against Marvel's own A–Z series index.

sections.title: Timely, 1941
sections.intro:
Simon and Kirby's first issue: cover-dated March 1941, on sale in December 1940, a year before the United States entered the war it is about.

Nothing later on this list needs it. It is here because it is the thing everything else is a revival of.

sections.title: The 1954 attempt
sections.intro:
Atlas brought the character back in 1954 for three issues and then stopped. They are filed under the same volume as the 1968 book, which is why the numbering here jumps from #78 to #100 — the #100 is inherited from Tales of Suspense rather than from these.

Skip them if you like. Englehart comes back to these three twenty years later and makes something of them, which is the only reason to have read them.

sections.title: The revival: Lee and Kirby
sections.intro:
Captain America had been out of print for a decade when the Avengers found him in 1964. Later that year he had half of Tales of Suspense, and for the next four years that is where the character lived, sharing a book with Iron Man.

The split matters for a practical reason. Only the back half of each Tales of Suspense is on this list, but Marvel files the whole issue under one cover, so you will be paging past an Iron Man story to get to it.

items.note: Not his own book — the issue that brings him back.
The strip starts here, in the back half of the book.
Kirby draws the origin again for the new readers.

sections.title: His own book again
sections.sub: #100–109 · straight on from Tales of Suspense · 1968–69
sections.intro: Tales of Suspense stops at #99 and Captain America carries its numbering on, which is why his first solo issue in fourteen years is #100.

items.note: Continues Tales of Suspense's numbering.

sections.title: Steranko
sections.sub: #110–113 · three issues, and the fill-in between them · 1969
sections.intro:
Jim Steranko wrote and drew three issues of this book and then left, and people have been talking about them ever since. They look like nothing else in 1969 Marvel.

#112 is a Lee and Kirby fill-in that landed in the middle of them. It is here because the numbering runs through it, not because the three need it.

items.note: Steranko.
Steranko.
A Lee and Kirby fill-in between Steranko's two halves.
Steranko's last.

sections.title: Lee winds down
sections.intro: Three years of a book with no particular direction, handed between writers. There is good work in it and no reason to start here.

sections.title: The Englehart era
sections.sub: #153–186 · the run that made the book political · 1972–75
sections.intro:
Steve Englehart took a book about a soldier who believes in his country and wrote thirty-odd issues about what that belief costs when the country turns out not to deserve it. It was published while the Watergate hearings were on television.

He also goes back to the three 1954 issues and builds a story out of them, which is the trick everyone remembers. Reading #76–78 first is not required, but it is three issues.

items.note: Englehart's first.

sections.title: Six months in between
sections.intro: The stretch between Englehart leaving and Kirby arriving. Four writers in six issues, and it shows.

sections.title: Kirby comes back
sections.intro:
Kirby returned to the character he co-created in 1941 and wrote it himself, with nobody editing the ideas down. The result is loud, strange, enormously confident and completely unlike the run it follows.

People who want the Englehart book back tend to hate it. Take it on its own terms.

items.note: Kirby returns, writing and drawing.

sections.title: Many hands
sections.intro: Four years the book spent being kept alive rather than written. Roger McKenzie holds most of it together. Skippable in full.

sections.title: Stern and Byrne
sections.intro: Nine issues, and the run people reach for when they want to argue the character works small. Stern and Byrne rebuilt his supporting cast and his day job, and closed on a single-issue retelling of the origin for the character's fortieth anniversary.

items.note: Stern and Byrne begin.

sections.title: Five before DeMatteis
sections.intro: Fill-ins between two runs.

sections.title: J.M. DeMatteis
sections.sub: #261–300 · with David Kraft taking six of them · 1981–84
sections.intro: DeMatteis writes the character as somebody who would rather talk than fight, and builds the run around villains he can argue with. It is quieter than what comes after it and better than its reputation.

items.note: DeMatteis begins.

sections.title: Michael Carlin
sections.intro: Six issues holding the door for the longest run the book has had.

sections.title: Mark Gruenwald
sections.sub: #307–443 · ten years, the longest run on the title · 1985–95
sections.intro:
Ten years and 137 issues, which is more of this character than anyone else has written. Gruenwald knew the Marvel universe better than its editors did and used the book as a place to take its rules seriously: what the job is, who else has done it, what the government thinks it owns.

It is uneven over a decade, and it is the run to read if you want to know the character rather than the highlights.

items.note: Gruenwald begins. He stays ten years.

sections.title: Mark Waid arrives
sections.sub: #444–454 · eleven issues before the line was restarted · 1995–96
sections.intro: Waid and Ron Garney got eleven issues before Marvel handed the character to another studio, and spent them writing the straight version — the one that takes the shield at face value. They are back in two sections' time.

items.note: Waid's first.

sections.title: Heroes Reborn
sections.sub: vol. 2 #1–13 · a year in a separate universe · 1996–97
sections.intro:
Marvel outsourced four of its oldest books for a year and restarted them in a pocket universe. This is the Captain America one, by Rob Liefeld and then James Robinson.

It connects to nothing before it and nothing after it. Included because the numbering goes through it.

items.note: Relaunched outside the main continuity.

sections.title: Heroes Return: Waid again
sections.intro: The same creative team, the same continuity, two years later — the run from #444 continuing as though the year in between had not happened.

items.note: Waid and Garney pick it back up.
A one-issue fill-in between the two runs.

sections.title: Dan Jurgens
sections.sub: vol. 3 #25–50 · to the end of the volume · 2000–02
sections.intro: Competent superhero comics for two years. Nothing here is needed later.

items.note: Jurgens takes over.

sections.title: The 2002 relaunch
sections.sub: vol. 4 #1–32 · four writers in thirty-two issues · 2002–04
sections.intro:
Marvel restarted the book in 2002 and pointed it squarely at the previous September. John Ney Rieber and John Cassaday open it; Chuck Austen, Dave Gibbons, Robert Morales and Robert Kirkman take the rest.

It argues with itself more than it works, and the next section is why anybody still buys this book.

items.note: Rieber and Cassaday relaunch it.

sections.title: Brubaker begins
sections.intro:
This is the reason most people arrive. Brubaker wrote the book for eight years and it reads as one continuous story — a spy thriller with a superhero in it, drawn mostly by Steve Epting in heavy shadow, where the plot turns on things that happened in 1945 and are still being paid for.

Start at #1. You need nothing above this line.

items.note: Brubaker's first. Eight years from here.

sections.title: Brubaker: the middle
sections.intro:
#22–24 are Civil War chapters. They are on the Civil War list here rather than on this one, in the interleaved order that event reads in, so the run steps from #21 to #25 and the gap is where they go.

The story is continuous across it either way.

items.note: #22-24 are Civil War chapters and sit on that list.

sections.title: Brubaker: the third act
sections.intro: Eight issues, and the last under this numbering.

sections.title: Back to the old numbering
sections.sub: vol. 5 #600–619, with the Reborn miniseries in its place · 2009–11
sections.intro: Marvel counted the whole title's issues and jumped to #600. The six-issue Reborn book ran alongside it and is slotted in where it was published, between #601 and #602.

items.note: 104 pages, and the old numbering is back.
A stand-alone, drawn by Gene Colan.
A six-issue book running alongside the main title.

sections.title: Volume six
sections.intro: Back to #1, with the same writer carrying straight on from #619. Nineteen issues.

items.note: Renumbered again; same writer, straight on.

sections.title: Captain America and Bucky
sections.sub: #620–628 · a companion book on the old numbering · 2011–12
sections.intro: Brubaker co-wrote nine issues of a second book, which keeps the legacy numbering going while volume six restarts at #1. The main run does not depend on it.

sections.title: Winter Soldier
sections.intro: The last fourteen issues Brubaker wrote of this story, in a book with somebody else's name on the cover. It is a spy comic with the superheroes almost entirely out of frame, and it is the end of the thing that started at volume five #1.

items.note: A book of its own, and where the run ends.
